notes: This is the review's PRIMARY effectiveness outcome and the correct decision-relevant quantity. Only 8 of the 15 studies in the systematic review could be pooled, because the other trials reported live birth only after the first transfer. Shi 2018 and Stormlund 2020 are therefore NOT in this cumulative estimate. Sensitivity analysis restricted to studies without selection-bias risk gave OR 1.09 (0.95 to 1.23), I2=0%, and the review reports this as '4 RCTs, 4328 women' although five trials are named in that sentence (Chen 2016, Santos-Ribeiro 2020, Vuong 2018, Wei 2019, Wong 2021) - an internal inconsistency in the published text. Corresponding RR was 1.03 (95% CI 0.99 to 1.08). This is the latest Cochrane version; see notes on absence of pub4.
A_what_is_wrong: Nothing material. I attacked the timing specifically and it holds: Cochrane's Methods define the primary outcome as 'Effectiveness: cumulative live birth rate per randomised woman. That is, the rate of live birth following the transfer of all (fresh or cryopreserved) embryos within the time horizon of the follow-up defined by the authors of the original study' - so the denominator really is the randomised woman and the numerator really is cumulative, not first-transfer. VISUAL READ of Figure 4 (rendered by me): cleavage subgroup Chen 2016 465/746 vs 455/762 OR 1.12 [0.91,1.37], Ferraretti 1999 23/58 vs 26/67 OR 1.04 [0.50,2.13], Vuong 2018 191/391 vs 185/391 OR 1.06 [0.80,1.41], subtotal 1.09 [0.93,1.29] I2=0%; blastocyst subgroup Santos-Ribeiro 2020 65/90 vs 67/94 OR 1.05 [0.55,1.99], Shapiro 2011a 37/70 vs 35/67 OR 1.03 [0.52,2.00], Shapiro 2011b 37/60 vs 39/62 OR 0.95 [0.46,1.97], Wei 2019 627/825 vs 604/825 OR 1.16 [0.93,1.45], Wong 2021 18/102 vs 29/102 OR 0.54 [0.28,1.05], subtotal 1.06 [0.88,1.27] I2=14%; Total 2342 vs 2370, events 1463 vs 1440, diamond 1.08 [0.95,1.22] straddling the null, Chi2=4.83 df=7 P=0.68 I2=0%, Z=1.21 (P=0.23), subgroup difference Chi2=0.07 df=1 P=0.78. Arm counts divide correctly (1463/2342=62.5%, 1440/2370=60.8%) and 2342+2370=4712; subgroup totals 1195+1220=2415 and 1147+1150=2297 both match. Summary of findings 1 reads '579 per 1000 | 589 per 1000 (567 to 627) | OR 1.08 (0.95 to 1.22) | 4712 (8 RCTs) | Moderate', so the claim's +1.0 pp (-1.2 to +4.8) derivation is right. Abstract confirms 'We included 15 studies in the systematic review and eight studies with a total of 4712 women in the meta-analysis' and the sensitivity-analysis internal inconsistency the claim flags is real: the text names five trials (Chen 2016; Santos-Ribeiro 2020; Vuong 2018; Wei 2019; Wong 2021) but says '4 RCTs, 4328 women'. Crossref probe shows CD011184.pub4 returns 404, so pub3 (2021-02-04) is genuinely the latest version. ONE MINOR GLOSS: the claim paraphrases cumulative as 'all transfers arising from one oocyte retrieval'; Cochrane actually says 'within the time horizon of the follow-up defined by the authors of the original study'. These coincide for the constituent trials but are not the same words.

Here, one could consider the result of the first embryo transfer in the frozen group against the combined outcomes of the fresh transfer and the first frozen-thawed-transfer in the fresh group. Therefore cumulative live birth rate is the relevant outcome for women.

notes: CRITICAL FOR SQ1: this is the single clearest demonstration that the per-transfer and cumulative framings give different answers from the same review and largely the same trials. Per-transfer is statistically positive with I2=74%; cumulative is null with I2=0%. Cochrane's own footnote states the per-transfer comparison is biased against the conventional arm because, at the time of the freeze-all arm's first transfer, the conventional arm would already have had a second transfer. Note Wei 2019 enters this analysis as 439/825 vs 341/825 (all live births), not the 416/825 vs 329/825 SINGLETON livebirth figure that is the Lancet paper's primary outcome.
A_what_is_wrong: Nothing material. Footnote a is a verbatim match, so the 'illustrative secondary analysis' characterisation is the review's own. VISUAL READ of Analysis 3.1 confirms every cell the claim reports: Aflatoonian 2018 33/121 vs 31/119 OR 1.06 [0.60,1.89]; Aghahosseini 2017 15/36 vs 15/36 OR 1.00 [0.39,2.55]; Chen 2016 368/746 vs 320/762 OR 1.34 [1.10,1.65] (19.0%); Coates 2017 47/61 vs 27/46 OR 2.36 [1.02,5.46]; Ferraretti 1999 23/58 vs 26/67 OR 1.04 [0.50,2.13]; Santos-Ribeiro 2020 42/104 vs 41/105 OR 1.06 [0.61,1.84]; Shapiro 2011a 23/70 vs 10/67 OR 2.79 [1.21,6.44]; Shapiro 2011b 1/62 vs 15/60 OR 0.05 [0.01,0.39] with the arrow running off the left of the plot; Shi 2018 525/1077 vs 542/1080 OR 0.94 [0.80,1.12] (32.8%, largest weight); Stormlund 2020 61/223 vs 66/230 OR 0.94 [0.62,1.41]; Vuong 2018 132/391 vs 123/391 OR 1.11 [0.82,1.50]; Wei 2019 439/825 vs 341/825 OR 1.61 [1.33,1.96] (18.9%); Wong 2021 7/102 vs 22/102 OR 0.27 [0.11,0.66]. Total 3876 vs 3890 (=7766), events 1716 vs 1579, diamond 1.17 [1.06,1.28] lying wholly right of the null; Chi2=46.47 df=12 P<0.00001 I2=74%; Z=3.27 (P=0.001). Crude OR from the totals is 1.163 with 95% CI 1.06-1.27, so the pooled M-H 1.17 (1.06-1.28) is coherent with the arm counts. The five extra trials are named in Table 1 exactly as the claim says. TWO NUANCES, neither a misrepresentation: (a) Cochrane's denominator is 'per randomised woman', not per transfer - the claim's own prose says 'per randomised woman', so the 'per-transfer' tag is a taxonomy label for the first-transfer epoch rather than a denominator statement; (b) Shapiro 2011b's arm totals are swapped between Analysis 1.1 (37/60 vs 39/62) and Analysis 3.1 (1/62 vs 15/60) - that inconsistency is Cochrane's, and the claim transcribes both correctly.

notes: This is the trial most often cited as establishing freeze-all superiority, and the effect is PER FIRST TRANSFER ONLY. Population is PCOS - not the whole population - so it does not by itself answer SQ1; it is included because it dominates the per-transfer pooled estimate and because its own cumulative result (SQ1-C4) contradicts the per-transfer headline. Mechanism reported by the authors was lower pregnancy loss (22.0% vs 32.7%), not higher implantation. DET design. Preeclampsia was higher after frozen transfer (4.4% vs 1.4%).
A_what_is_wrong: Nothing. Verbatim match. The timing is explicitly first-transfer and is stated twice by the trial itself: Methods - 'The primary outcome was a live birth, which was defined as delivery of any viable infant at 28 weeks or more of gestation during the first embryo transfer'; Abstract - 'Frozen-embryo transfer resulted in a higher frequency of live birth after the first transfer than did fresh-embryo transfer'. Population verbatim: 'A total of 1508 infertile women with the polycystic ovary syndrome who were undergoing their first IVF cycle were randomly assigned...All the women were between the ages of 20 and 34 years and weighed at least 40 kg' and 'Enrollment began in June 2013 and was completed in May 2014 at 14 reproductive medical centers throughout China'. DET verbatim: 'After 3 days of embryo development, women underwent the transfer of up to two fresh or frozen embryos.' The arm counts 368/746 and 320/762 are not printed in the NEJM text I obtained (Table 3 body did not come through), but the claim explicitly flags them as Cochrane-sourced, and I independently verified them in Cochrane Analysis 3.1 which I rendered and read myself; they reproduce 49.3% and 42.0% exactly and my recomputed RR is 1.175 with 95% CI 1.05-1.31, an exact match to the published CI.

notes: Load-bearing for SQ1: the flagship 'freeze-all wins' trial reports internally that the win does not survive the shift from per-transfer to cumulative accounting. The authors themselves make the point in the Discussion: 'Our observation that there was no significant between-group difference in cumulative live-birth rates underscores the efficacy of subsequent frozen-embryo transfer among women in whom fresh-embryo transfer was not successful.' A_what_is_wrong: Nothing. Verbatim match, and the direction of the claim (per-first-transfer win does not survive cumulative accounting) is the authors' own reading: Discussion - 'Our observation that there was no significant between-group difference in cumulative live-birth rates underscores the efficacy of subsequent frozen-embryo transfer among women in whom fresh-embryo transfer was not successful.' The claim's assertion that cumulative was prespecified rather than a post hoc rescue is also correct: Methods - 'Prespecified secondary outcomes included biochemical pregnancy, clinical pregnancy, ongoing pregnancy, singleton live birth, cumulative live birth (including subsequent frozen-embryo transfer), pregnancy loss...'. population: 1650 women with regular menstrual cycles undergoing their first cycle of in-vitro fertilisation, enrolled Aug 1 2016 to June 3 2017 at 21 academic fertility centres in China; described by the authors as ovulatory women with good prognosis
embryos_transferred: SET - single blastocyst in both arms ('elective frozen single blastocyst transfer'; 'a delayed frozen-thawed single blastocyst transfer was done')
absolute_risk_difference: NOT reported as an absolute difference with CI in the text available to me. COMPUTED BY ME from the reported counts: 416/825 (50.4%) minus 329/825 (39.9%) = +10.5 percentage points.
quote: 825 women were assigned to each group and included in analyses. Frozen single blastocyst transfer resulted in higher rates of singleton livebirth than did fresh single blastocyst transfer (416 [50%] vs 329 [40%]; relative risk [RR] 1.26, 95% CI 1.14-1.41, p<0.0001).
location: Summary, Findings (publisher page); corresponds to the trial's primary outcome
retrieval_path: FAILED to obtain full text. Tried: (1) Unpaywall - oa_status 'closed'; (2) Semantic Scholar - isOpenAccess false, no openAccessPdf; (3) parallel-cli extract of the Lancet /fulltext URL - returned Summary sections only; (4) parallel-cli extract of the Lancet showPdf URL - again returned Summary only; (5) curl of publisher - blocked. The quoted Findings text is verbatim from the publisher's own page, so the primary-outcome numbers are primary-sourced, but the Results tables were not obtained.
notes: IMPORTANT DEFINITIONAL POINT: the primary outcome is SINGLETON livebirth, not all live birth. Cochrane's per-first-transfer analysis enters Wei 2019 as 439/825 vs 341/825 (all live births) and its cumulative analysis as 627/825 vs 604/825 - so the trial's headline 50% vs 40% is not the same quantity as either Cochrane cell pair. Since the fresh arm was also single-blastocyst, the singleton framing does not create the usual DET multiple-birth artefact, but the distinction still matters when pooling. This is the ONLY pivotal trial in an unselected/ovulatory population that is both SET and positive on live birth per transfer. I could not verify from the trial itself whether cumulative live birth was reported.
A_what_is_wrong: Nothing material. Verbatim match (the source uses middle-dot decimals). Population verbatim from the same record: 'This multicentre, non-blinded, randomised controlled trial was undertaken in 21 academic fertility centres in China. 1650 women with regular menstrual cycles undergoing their first cycle of in-vitro fertilisation were enrolled from Aug 1, 2016, to June 3, 2017'; SET verbatim: 'For those assigned to frozen blastocyst transfer, all blastocysts were cryopreserved and a delayed frozen-thawed single blastocyst transfer was done'; and the claim's important definitional caveat is the trial's own words: 'The primary outcome was singleton livebirth rate.' Arithmetic is exact: 416/825=50.4%, 329/825=39.9%, crude RR 1.264 with 95% CI 1.135-1.408 versus the published 1.26 (1.14-1.41). I attacked the first-transfer timing since the abstract never says 'first transfer', and it holds independently: Cochrane's Characteristics of included studies record for Wei 2019, which I read in my own PDF, states 'The primary outcome was singleton live birth rate' and lists 'the rate of cumulative live birth within 12 months after the first ET' among POST-HOC analyses - i.e. the headline 416/329 is the index-transfer quantity and the cumulative quantity is separate (Cochrane enters it as 627/825 vs 604/825). That same record also answers a question the claim left open ('I could not verify from the trial itself whether cumulative live birth was reported'): it was reported, post hoc, with follow-up defined as 'cumulative ongoing pregnancy rate and LBR (including all FETs performed within the 12 months after the initial transfer)'. LIMITATION ON MY SIDE: I could not read the Lancet Results tables, so I verified the headline numbers and the timing but not the table-level cell counts.

claim: In 460 women aged 18-39 with regular menstrual cycles at eight public hospitals in Denmark, Sweden and Spain, a freeze-all strategy with GnRH-agonist trigger and single frozen blastocyst transfer gave no difference in live birth after the first transfer versus fresh single blastocyst transfer: 61/223 (27.4%) versus 66/230 (28.7%), risk ratio 0.98 (95% CI 0.87 to 1.10), P=0.83.
population: 460 women aged 18-39 years with regular menstrual cycles starting their first, second, or third treatment cycle of IVF or ICSI; outpatient fertility clinics at eight public hospitals in Denmark, Sweden and Spain; enrolled 5 May 2016 to 7 September 2018
embryos_transferred: SET - single blastocyst in both arms (freeze-all arm: single frozen-thawed blastocyst in a subsequent modified natural cycle; fresh arm: single blastocyst in the fresh cycle)
absolute_risk_difference: NOT reported for live birth (the paper reports it for the primary outcome, ongoing pregnancy: -1.8, 95% CI -10.5 to 7.0). COMPUTED BY ME for live birth: 27.4% minus 28.7% = -1.3 percentage points.
quote: No significant difference was found in the live birth rate between the freeze-all and fresh transfer group (61 of 223 (27.4%) and 66 of 230 (28.7%), respectively; risk ratio 0.98, 95% confidence interval 0.87 to 1.10, P=0.83; table 3 ).
location: Results; table 3 (Reproductive outcomes for women in freeze-all and fresh transfer groups, intention-to-treat)
retrieval_path: Europe PMC REST fullTextXML for PMC7399608 (121 KB JATS XML) saved to ./figs_source/stormlund2020_fulltext.xml; parsed with Python. Direct curl of bmj.com PDF returned HTTP 403.
notes: EPOCH: this is a FIRST-TRANSFER-epoch outcome and belongs on the per-transfer side of the per-transfer/cumulative dichotomy, NOT the cumulative side; it is tagged 'per-woman-randomised' because the denominator is all randomised women who started stimulation and because the outcome counts natural conceptions occurring during the segmentation pause (five women, 2.3%, conceived naturally in the freeze-all group). The cumulative counterpart is SQ1-C10. Live birth was a SECONDARY outcome; the primary outcome was ongoing pregnancy (62/223, 27.8% vs 68/230, 29.6%; RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.10; P=0.76). Denominators are 223 and 230, not 230/230, because 460 were enrolled and randomised 230:230 but seven withdrew consent and were excluded, leaving 453 who started stimulation. IMPORTANT CONTAMINATION OF THE FRESH ARM: 30 women allocated to fresh transfer had transfer postponed to a subsequent frozen cycle per protocol (24 for OHSS risk, 6 for lack of blastocyst development on day five), plus 7 more for other reasons; only 1 woman allocated to freeze-all had a fresh transfer. This biases the comparison toward the null. Trial designed as a superiority study powered to detect a 13 percentage point difference - substantially over-optimistic, so it is underpowered for realistic effect sizes.
A_what_is_wrong: The headline claim is exactly right (number, population and timing all match), so the verdict is CONFIRMED - but TWO THINGS THE PARENT MUST NOT REPEAT UNCHECKED. (1) The claim's absolute_risk_difference field says the risk difference is 'NOT reported for live birth (the paper reports it for the primary outcome, ongoing pregnancy: -1.8, 95% CI -10.5 to 7.0). COMPUTED BY ME for live birth: 27.4% minus 28.7% = -1.3 percentage points.' That is FALSE. Table 3 reports it, with a confidence interval, in the very row the claim cites: 'Live birth rate/No of randomised women 61/223 (27.4) 66/230 (28.7) -1.3 (-10.1 to 7.4) 0.98 (0.87 to 1.10) 0.83'. The claim presents as its own computation a number the source prints, and omits the CI (-10.1 to 7.4) that the source supplies. (2) SOURCE-LEVEL ANOMALY, not the claim's fault but load-bearing if quoted: the published 'risk ratio 0.98 (0.87 to 1.10)' is not reproducible from 61/223 vs 66/230 - the crude risk ratio is 0.953 with an exact 95% CI of 0.71 to 1.28, so the published interval is far too narrow for a binomial risk ratio on these counts, and it is byte-identical to the ongoing-pregnancy row (62/223 vs 68/230, crude RR 0.939, also published as 0.98, 0.87 to 1.10). Do not present '61/223 vs 66/230; RR 0.98 (0.87-1.10)' as an internally coherent triple. Population verified verbatim: 'Setting Outpatient fertility clinics at eight public hospitals in Denmark, Sweden, and Spain. Participants 460 women aged 18-39 years with regular menstrual cycles starting their first, second, or third treatment cycle of in vitro fertilisation or intracytoplasmic sperm injection.' The claim's careful 'per-woman-randomised' tag is justified: table 3 gives four denominators (randomised women 61/223, started stimulation 61/223, oocyte retrievals 61/221, embryo transfers 56/162) and the claim uses the randomised-woman one, with the 5-woman gap between 61 and 56 explained by 'Five women (2.3%) in the freeze-all group conceived naturally during the pause between oocyte retrieval and blastocyst transfer'. Contamination of the fresh arm verified verbatim (24 women postponed for OHSS risk, six for lack of blastocyst development, seven more for other reasons, 'Only one woman randomised to the freeze-all group had fresh embryo transfer'). Timing is first-transfer-epoch and not cumulative, confirmed by the paper itself: 'Cumulative live birth rates including time to delivery in the cumulative cycles, detailed embryo data, and evaluation of cost effectiveness will be accounted for in separate publications.'

claim: In the same Danish/Swedish/Spanish trial followed for a minimum of two years, the CUMULATIVE live birth rate combining all frozen transfers from the same oocyte retrieval was 95/223 (42.6%) with freeze-all versus 96/230 (41.7%) with the fresh strategy, risk ratio 1.0 (95% CI 0.87 to 1.19), P=0.93, while median time to first pregnancy was 106.0 days versus 29.0 days.
population: Same 460 women aged 18-39 with regular menstrual cycles randomised 1:1 in the multicentre trial; minimum follow-up two years from the start of ovarian stimulation
design: multicentre RCT (prespecified secondary outcome reported in a separate paper)
embryos_transferred: SET - single blastocyst for the index transfer in both arms, plus all subsequent vitrified-warmed transfers from the same retrieval
absolute_risk_difference: NOT reported as an absolute difference with CI. COMPUTED BY ME: 42.6% minus 41.7% = +0.9 percentage points.
quote: Combining all FET from the included oocyte retrievals, the cumulative live birth rate was 42.6% (95/223) in the freeze-all group versus 41.7% (96/230) in the fresh strategy group (risk ratio 1.0, 95% CI 0.87-1.19; P = 0.93).
location: Abstract, Results (publisher page, Reproductive BioMedicine Online)
retrieval_path: Unpaywall reports oa_status 'closed'. parallel-cli extract of https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rbmo.2024.104449 returned the structured abstract verbatim from the publisher page plus reference list, but not the Results body or tables. Saved to ./figs_source/stormlund2025_extract.json.
notes: This is the cumulative counterpart to SQ1-C9 and post-dates the Cochrane review, so it is NOT in any published meta-analysis. Quantifies the time cost of segmentation directly: median (IQR) time to first pregnancy 106.0 (80.5-156.5) days with freeze-all versus 29.0 (27.0-113.5) days with fresh. Deliveries from subsequent FET cycles were similar (15.2%, 34/223 vs 12.6%, 29/230; P=0.5). Same 223/230 denominators as the index paper, so the seven consent withdrawals remain excluded.
A_what_is_wrong: Nothing material. Verbatim match, and I attacked the timing hard because this is the claim most exposed to cumulative/per-transfer confusion. It survives: the title is 'Cumulative live birth rates in a freeze-all or fresh transfer strategy after one ART cycle in ovulatory women', the research question is 'Are cumulative live birth rates similar following a freeze-all strategy compared with a fresh transfer strategy including all subsequent vitrified-warmed cycles from the same oocyte retrieval?', and the follow-up is 'The minimum follow-up time from the start of ovarian stimulation was 2 years' - genuinely cumulative, genuinely per woman randomised, and the same 223/230 denominators as the 2020 index paper. Arithmetic checks: 95/223=42.6%, 96/230=41.7%, crude RR 1.021, RD +0.9 pp. Design descriptor verified: 'The study related to the secondary outcome in a multicentre randomized controlled trial including 460 women allocated in a 1:1 ratio', which corroborates the claim's 'prespecified secondary outcome reported in a separate paper' and dovetails with the 2020 paper's own promise of separate cumulative publications. The notes' extra numbers are also verbatim: median time to first pregnancy 106.0 (80.5-156.5) versus 29.0 (27.0-113.5) days, and deliveries from subsequent FET cycles 15.2% (34/223) versus 12.6% (29/230), P=0.5. ONE FLAG, same as SQ1-C9 and again a source-level property rather than a claim error: the published 95% CI 0.87-1.19 is narrower than the exact binomial interval for these counts (0.82 to 1.27), so this group's reported risk-ratio intervals should not be re-derived from the cell counts.

claim: In the E-Freeze pragmatic multicentre UK trial of 619 couples across 18 clinics - an unselected IVF/ICSI population and the only major trial published after the Cochrane search date - elective freeze did not improve live birth after the first embryo transfer and the point estimate favoured fresh: 87/307 (28.3%) versus 106/309 (34.3%), adjusted risk ratio 0.83 (99% CI 0.65 to 1.06).
population: 619 couples undergoing their first, second or third cycle of IVF/ICSI treatment with at least three good quality embryos on Day 3, female partner aged 18 to under 42 years, across 18 UK clinics 2016-2019; couples using donor gametes, undergoing preimplantation genetic testing, or already planning to freeze all embryos were excluded
embryos_transferred: Predominantly SET but not exclusively: 'Over 80% of women in both randomized groups received a single embryo; the others received two embryos, with the exception of one woman who had a triple embryo transfer.' Most transfers were at blastocyst stage (94.6% frozen, 93.1% fresh).
absolute_risk_difference: REPORTED BY THE PAPER in the economic analysis: live birth rate difference -0.06 (95% CI -0.127 to 0.020), i.e. -6.0 percentage points, lower in the elective freeze arm. Consistent with my own computation from the Table II counts: 28.3% minus 34.3% = -6.0 percentage points.
quote: The live birth rate {28.3% versus 34.3%; RR, 99% CI: 0.83 (0.65 to 1.06)} and clinical pregnancy rates {33.9% versus 40.1%; RR, 99% CI: 0.85 (0.65 to 1.11)} were lower in the elective freeze arm, but there is no statistically significant difference ( Table II ).
location: Results; Table II 'Primary and secondary outcomes of the E-Freeze trial', row 'Live birth episode | 87 (28.3%) | 106 (34.3%) | 0.83 (0.61 to 1.13) | 0.83 (0.65 to 1.06) | 0.054'
retrieval_path: Europe PMC REST fullTextXML for PMC9206534 (111 KB JATS XML) saved to ./figs_source/efreeze2022_fulltext.xml; Table II parsed from the XML with Python.
notes: NOT IN THE COCHRANE REVIEW - published March 2022, after Cochrane's search date of 23 September 2020. It is the only large trial in a genuinely unselected Western population and it points, non-significantly, the OTHER way. The CI is a 99% CI because secondary outcomes were adjusted for multiplicity; the unadjusted 95% RR was 0.83 (0.61 to 1.13) and P=0.054. Live birth was a SECONDARY outcome; the primary outcome was healthy baby rate after first transfer (62/307, 20.3% vs 75/309, 24.4%; RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.15). MAJOR CAVEAT: adherence in the elective freeze arm was poor owing to patient preference for fresh transfer, though complier-average-causal-effect (0.77, 0.44 to 1.10), per-protocol (0.87, 0.59 to 1.26) and as-treated (0.91, 0.64 to 1.29) analyses were all consistent. The trial did not reach its planned sample size of 1086. NO cumulative data: 'We have not reported on cumulative healthy baby rate in this manuscript as that is a follow-up study.' Elective freeze was also more costly (+GBP 170, 95% CI 67 to 289) and unlikely to be cost-effective in the NHS.
A_what_is_wrong: The headline claim is exactly right and the verdict is CONFIRMED. Table II row read verbatim: 'Live birth episode | 87 (28.3%) | 106 (34.3%) | 0.83 (0.61 to 1.13) | 0.83 (0.65 to 1.06) | 0.054', under headers 'Unadjusted risk ratio (95 or 99% CI)' and 'Adjusted* risk ratio (95 or 99% CI)'. Population verbatim: 'A pragmatic two-arm parallel randomized controlled trial (E-Freeze) was conducted across 18 clinics in the UK from 2016 to 2019. A total of 619 couples were randomized (309 to elective freeze/310 to fresh)' and 'Couples undergoing their first, second or third cycle of IVF/ICSI treatment, with at least three good quality embryos on Day 3 where the female partner was >=18 and <42 years of age were eligible. Those using donor gametes, undergoing preimplantation genetic testing or planning to freeze all their embryos were excluded.' Timing is first-transfer and the absence of cumulative data is the authors' own statement: 'We have not reported on cumulative healthy baby rate in this manuscript as that is a follow-up study.' The economic-analysis risk difference the claim cites is verbatim: 'the healthy baby rate (-0.039, 95% CI -0.101 to 0.027) and live birth rate (-0.06, 95% CI: -0.127 to 0.020) were lower in the elective freeze than fresh transfer arm'. ONE ERROR IN THE CLAIM'S NOTES, which the parent should fix before reuse: the notes say 'the unadjusted 95% RR was 0.83 (0.61 to 1.13)'. That interval is a 99% CI, not 95%. The table footnote states 'CIs are 95% for the primary outcome and 99% for all secondary outcomes', live birth is a secondary outcome, and my recomputation settles it - the crude 99% CI on 87/307 vs 106/309 is 0.606 to 1.126, which rounds to exactly (0.61, 1.13), whereas the crude 95% CI would be (0.65, 1.05). A second, smaller notes imprecision: the claim lists CACE/per-protocol/as-treated results without saying they belong to the primary outcome, but the paper restricts them - 'Further pre-specified analyses were carried out for the primary outcome only: complier-average causal effect analysis; per-protocol...and as-treated'.
B_what_is_wrong: The live-birth counts and adjusted RR are present, but this was not an unselected IVF/ICSI population: randomisation occurred only after at least three good-quality Day-3 embryos were available. Of 1578 consented couples, 959 were not randomised, including 476 because three good-quality embryos were unavailable. The effect metadata also mislabels 0.65 to 1.06 as a 95% CI; Table II specifies a 99% CI for this secondary outcome. Finally, the 'only major trial published after the Cochrane search date' assertion is no longer true: a 2025 BMJ multicentre freeze-all-versus-fresh RCT randomised 838 women with low IVF prognosis (https://www.bmj.com/content/388/bmj-2024-081474).

claim: As of this search there is NO published individual-participant-data meta-analysis of freeze-all versus fresh transfer: the INFORM IPD meta-analysis exists only as a protocol (BMJ Open 2022, PROSPERO CRD42021296566), with live birth resulting from the first embryo transfer as its planned primary outcome.
outcome: live birth per transfer (first transfer) - planned, not yet reported
population: Planned: couples undergoing IVF in RCTs comparing a freeze-all embryo transfer strategy and a fresh embryo transfer strategy
design: IPD meta-analysis (protocol only - no results published)
embryos_transferred: Not applicable - protocol
absolute_risk_difference: Not applicable - no results have been published.
quote: Existing randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing a freeze-all embryo transfer strategy and a fresh embryo transfer strategy have shown conflicting results. A freeze-all or a fresh transfer policy may be preferable for some couples undergoing in-vitro fertilisation (IVF), but it is unclear which couples would benefit most from each policy, how and under which protocols. Therefore, we plan a systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis of RCTs comparing a freeze-all and a fresh transfer policy.
location: Abstract, Introduction and Methods-and-analysis sections of the protocol
retrieval_path: PubMed efetch XML for PMID 35851030 (structured abstract, author list, PROSPERO ID). Searched for results publications by: PubMed IPD-plus-freeze-all term combinations (3 hits, none a results paper); PubMed author search on Wang R and McLernon D restricted to 2022 onward with freeze-all terms (5 hits, none a results paper); OpenAlex reviews citing E-Freeze (10 hits, the only INFORM item being the 2022 protocol itself). No results publication found.
notes: Directly answers the brief's question 'Any individual-participant-data meta-analysis'. The author list includes the principal investigators of the pivotal trials (Chen, Wei, Legro, Sun, Wu, Vuong, Pinborg, Stormlund) plus Showell and McLernon, so this is the trialist-led IPD effort, not a third-party one. Its planned primary outcome is live birth after the FIRST transfer, which is the timing Cochrane deprecates - worth flagging, because the IPD will therefore not by itself resolve the cumulative question. Search was performed 23 September 2020 per the protocol and was to be updated. This record exists so a verifier can confirm the absence of results rather than assume it.
A_what_is_wrong: The claim's central assertion is refuted. It states 'As of this search there is NO published individual-participant-data meta-analysis of freeze-all versus fresh transfer: the INFORM IPD meta-analysis exists only as a protocol'. INFORM results are published, in three places, and the most SQ1-relevant one reports precisely the outcome this sub-question is about. (1) Fertility and Sterility, October 2024, DOI 10.1016/j.fertnstert.2024.07.251, 'WHO BENEFITS MOST FROM A FREEZE-ALL EMBRYO TRANSFER STRATEGY? AN INDIVIDUAL PARTICIPANT DATA META-ANALYSIS OF RANDOMISED CONTROLLED TRIALS (INFORM)', Wang R, Au LS, Wei D, ... Legro RS, Wang Z, Sun Y, Wu K, Vuong LN et al: 'The primary outcome was live birth following the first transfer', results as quoted above, and 'CONCLUSIONS The freeze-all and fresh embryo transfer strategies did not differ significantly in overall live birth rate following the first transfer, although a freeze-only strategy benefitted patients with elevated progesterone levels on trigger day.' (2) Human Reproduction 40(Supplement_1), June 2025, DOI 10.1093/humrep/deaf097.1086, 'P-782 Obstetric and Neonatal Outcomes following Freeze-all vs Fresh Embryo Transfer Strategies: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis of Randomised Trials (INFORM)' (Au N, Wang R, Wei D, Vuong LN, Pinborg AB et al), 12 RCTs, 8222 participants, hypertensive disorders 2.9% vs 1.8% aRR 1.66, LGA 17.8% vs 13.1% aRR 1.38, SGA 5.7% vs 8.1% aRR 0.71, and it states in terms 'Our earlier work on this IPD-MA found no significant live birth rate differences between the two groups'. (3) A full results manuscript is posted as a 2026 preprint, DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7001926, 'Frozen Versus Fresh Embryo Transfer in IVF - An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials (INFORM)', with the full INFORM author list and the same PROSPERO registration CRD42021296566: search 'up until 24 September 2025', 'Among 16 eligible trials, IPD from 13 trials involving 9060 randomised participants (96% of eligible participants) were obtained', primary outcome 'live birth following the first embryo transfer', result 'no evidence that a freeze-all embryo transfer strategy differed from a fresh embryo transfer on live birth rate following the first transfer (adjusted risk ratio (aRR) 1.00, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.86 to 1.17, moderate-certainty evidence)', plus OHSS aRR 0.28 (0.18 to 0.43, high certainty) and major congenital anomaly aRR 0.73 (0.63 to 0.85), and the interpretation 'In unselected IVF population, the freeze-all and fresh embryo transfer strategies are comparable in terms of live birth rate following the first transfer'. WHY THE CLAIM MISSED IT: its stated search used PubMed and OpenAlex only, and neither indexes ASRM/ESHRE abstracts published in Fertility and Sterility or Human Reproduction supplements, nor SSRN preprints; the Europe PMC citation list for the protocol has just one entry. WHY THIS MATTERS FOR SQ1, beyond the bibliographic point: the claim's own note argues 'the IPD will therefore not by itself resolve the cumulative question'. That framing now needs revising, because the IPD result on the per-first-transfer outcome is NULL (aRR 1.00, 0.86-1.17 in the full analysis; 1.04, 0.92-1.18 in the earlier 12-trial version) and therefore directly contradicts Cochrane's pooled per-first-transfer OR 1.17 (1.06-1.28) with I2=74% - the IPD analysis, adjusted for age and BMI and using 96% of eligible participants, brings the per-transfer estimate into line with the cumulative null rather than leaving the two timings in conflict. WHAT SURVIVES: the protocol itself is real and correctly described - I verified via Europe PMC that BMJ Open 2022 PMID 35851030 states 'The primary outcome will be live birth resulting from the first embryo transfer', that PROSPERO registration is CRD42021296566, and that 'The search was performed on 23 September 2020 and will be updated'. The quote the claim attributes to the protocol is verbatim.
B_what_is_wrong: The 2022 protocol and its planned first-transfer primary outcome are real, but the categorical statement that INFORM exists only as a protocol and has published no results is false. Fertility and Sterility published this INFORM primary-results abstract in October 2024. Human Reproduction also published an INFORM obstetric/neonatal IPD-results abstract in June 2025 (https://academic.oup.com/humrep/article/40/Supplement_1/deaf097.1086/8170259). I did not need to infer that a full-length results article exists: these published results abstracts alone refute 'no results have been published.'

claim: In a Cochrane meta-analysis of 6 RCTs (4478 women) comparing a 'freeze all' strategy with conventional IVF/ICSI including fresh transfer, elective freeze-all reduced ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome per randomised woman (17/2226 vs 83/2252; Peto OR 0.26, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.39, I2 = 0%), an absolute reduction of 2.92 percentage points (3.69% to 0.76%).
outcome_definition: OHSS per randomised woman, pooled across trials using each trial's own definition; the review notes 'Definitions of OHSS vary widely in literature as in the included studies' and that two studies (Ferraretti 1999; Wong 2021) 'reported on OHSS per woman if hospitalisation was required'. Forest-plot subgroup label: '1.2.1 Per cycle with ovarian hyperstimulation'.
population: Women undergoing autologous IVF/ICSI randomised to freeze-all versus conventional fresh-transfer strategy; pooled trials span PCOS (Chen 2016), ovulatory good-prognosis (Wei 2019), non-PCOS (Vuong 2018), high responders (Santos-Ribeiro 2020), women at high OHSS risk (Ferraretti 1999) and unselected (Wong 2021)
trigger: as stated - varies by trial; hCG in Chen 2016, Vuong 2018, Wei 2019; GnRH agonist in BOTH arms in Santos-Ribeiro 2020
high_risk_excluded: as stated - varies by trial; Shapiro 2011a and Shapiro 2011b were EXCLUDED from this analysis because 'women with high risk of OHSS were excluded and received the freeze all strategy as standard'
absolute_risk_difference: COMPUTED BY ME from the forest-plot arm counts: 17/2226 = 0.76% vs 83/2252 = 3.69%, ARD = -2.92 percentage points, NNT = 34. The review's own Summary of Findings expresses this as 33 per 1000 with conventional IVF versus 9 per 1000 (6 to 13) with freeze-all, i.e. ARD approximately -2.4 percentage points; the review's plain-language statement is 'if the OHSS rate is 3% following a conventional IVF/ICSI strategy, the rate following a freeze all strategy would be 1%'.
quote: Women might develop less OHSS after the 'freeze all' strategy compared to the conventional IVF/ICSI strategy (OR 0.26, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.39; I2 = 0%; 6 RCTs, 4478 women; low-quality evidence). These data suggest that for an OHSS rate of 3% following the conventional strategy, the rate following the 'freeze all' strategy would be 1%.
location: Abstract, Main results; and Results section 1.2 'Safety: ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) per woman'; Analysis 1.2; Figure 5 (PDF page 24, printed page 21)

notes: CRITICAL SCOPE LIMIT: this pooled OHSS estimate does NOT include Shi 2018 (n=2157), Stormlund 2020 (n=460) or E-Freeze 2022 (n=619) - Shi 2018 and Stormlund 2020 were used by the review only in an additional live-birth-after-first-transfer analysis, and E-Freeze postdates the 23 Sept 2020 search close. Adding those three trials would attenuate the pooled estimate, because all three reported small or non-significant OHSS differences. The evidence was graded LOW quality by the review authors. Mixed SET/DET and cleavage/blastocyst. notes: E-Freeze is in NO meta-analysis - it postdates the Cochrane search close of 23 Sept 2020. It is the single most important trial for the question of whether freeze-all reduces OHSS in an UNSELECTED population under routine practice, and its answer is: point estimate favours freeze-all with the same magnitude as the pooled RCT estimate (RR 0.44), but it does not reach significance and the trial concluded 'The risk of OHSS was not reduced by an elective freeze policy.' Two design features blunt the comparison: hCG was given to essentially everyone because randomisation was deferred to day 3 after fertilisation, and women with a clinical indication for freezing were excluded. Adherence to allocation was poor in the elective freeze arm. Trial did not reach its full planned sample size. A_what_is_wrong: The headline is exact - 'The risk of OHSS was 3.6% (11/307) in the elective freeze arm compared to 8.1% (25/309) in the fresh embryo transfer arm (RR 0.44, 99% CI: 0.15 to 1.30) (Table II). The severity of ovarian hyperstimulation was only mild to moderate in the elective freeze group, whereas there were 6 cases (1.9%) of severe OHSS in the fresh embryo transfer group' is verbatim, 619 couples across 18 UK clinics 2016-2019 is verbatim, single embryo transfer 249/298 (83.6%) and 247/303 (81.5%) confirms 'over 80%', the exclusion 'a clinical indication for an elective freeze such as OHSS or fertility preservation' is verbatim, and 'The risk of OHSS was not reduced by an elective freeze policy' is verbatim. WHAT IS WRONG is the claim's statistical annotation: 'the corresponding 95% CI given in the outcome table is 0.18 to 1.10'. It is not a 95% CI. Table II's own footnote states 'CIs are 95% for the primary outcome and 99% for all secondary outcomes', and OHSS is a secondary outcome, so 0.44 (0.18 to 1.10) is the UNADJUSTED RR with a 99% CI while 0.44 (0.15 to 1.30) is the ADJUSTED RR with a 99% CI - the claim has both mislabelled the interval level and conflated unadjusted with adjusted. I verified this arithmetically: for 11/307 vs 25/309, log-RR SE = 0.353, giving a 99% CI of 0.18 to 1.10 (matching the table exactly) and a 95% CI of 0.22 to 0.88. This is material, not cosmetic: the true 95% interval EXCLUDES 1, so the trial's 'non-significant' verdict rests entirely on its prespecified 99% intervals, and a reader relying on the claim's annotation would report a non-significant 95% CI that does not exist. The claim set is internally inconsistent on this point - SQ2-C14's notes correctly label the same column's preterm-delivery entry (0.91, 0.31 to 2.65) as a 99% CI.

The trigger differs by arm by design (GnRH agonist in freeze-all, hCG in fresh), so any OHSS difference here reflects trigger plus transfer strategy jointly, not transfer strategy alone. On top of that, the protocol applied a rescue freeze-all in the fresh arm for anyone with >18 follicles >=11 mm, which removed the very women who would have generated OHSS events. The net effect is that the trial cannot inform the OHSS question at all - and the authors say as much, framing the near-zero rates as a consequence of 'the strict criteria of our study design'. The authors also note that in previous trials using hCG triggering in the freeze-all group, OHSS risk in the freeze-all arm 'varied between 0.5% and 1.3%'. Every element of the claim - including the two features the claim says confound the comparison - is verbatim in the source: the trigger genuinely differs by arm by design, and the protocolised rescue freeze-all for >18 follicles >=11 mm genuinely removed 24/230 (10.4%) of the fresh arm for OHSS risk. The claim's outcome_definition field states the review prespecified HDP as 'Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, comprising pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH), pre-eclampsia (PE) and [eclampsia]'. notes: HIGH VALUE FOR SQ3, WITH TWO CAVEATS. (1) The two stratum estimates differ by 0.05 on the RR scale and their confidence intervals overlap almost completely; the normal-responder stratum also carries I-squared 77%. The review's own limitation statement concedes that 'the analysis did not apply a standard for determining high or normal responders since the type of ovarian response followed the characterisation of populations as reported by the authors of the eligible studies' - i.e. the stratification is a label inherited from the trials, not a measured covariate. Responder status is a proxy for, not identical to, PCOS status. (2) THE PUBLISHED ABSTRACT IS INTERNALLY INCONSISTENT ON STRATUM SIZES: it states four RCTs with n=2010 in high responders and four RCTs with n=3255 in normal responders, but then reports the live-birth analysis as three studies with n=3398 in high responders and three studies with n=1608 in normal responders. The larger n is attached to the smaller stratum, which suggests a transposition in the abstract. I could not retrieve the full text to resolve this, so the stratum sizes should be treated as unverified; the relative risks and confidence intervals are quoted verbatim and are the load-bearing numbers here.
A_what_is_wrong: The claim opens with a false uniqueness assertion: 'The ONLY meta-analysis that stratifies freeze-all versus fresh transfer by a physiological proxy for the PCOS/ovulatory axis (Bosdou 2019, by ovarian responder type)'. It is not the only one, and the other one predates it. Roque M, Haahr T, Geber S, Esteves SC, Humaidan P. 'Fresh versus elective frozen embryo transfer in IVF/ICSI cycles: a systematic review and meta-analysis of reproductive outcomes.' Hum Reprod Update 2019;25(1):2-14, PMID 30388233, doi 10.1093/humupd/dmy033, stratifies on exactly the same axis. Its abstract states verbatim: 'Subgroup analyses included normal and hyper-responder patients, embryo developmental stage on the day of embryo transfer, freezing method and the route of progesterone administration for luteal phase support in eFET cycles' and 'Subgroup analyses indicated higher LBRs by eFET than by fresh embryo transfer in hyper-responders (RR = 1.16; 95% CI: 1.05-1.28) and in PGT-A cycles (RR = 1.55; 95% CI: 1.14-2.10). However, no differences were observed for LBR in normo-responders (RR = 1.03; 95% CI: 0.91-1.17)'. On WebFetch of the Roque full text the strata are labelled explicitly as 'PCOS/hyper-responder patients' versus 'non-PCOS/normo-responders' with 4 studies/2035 patients and 3 studies/3076 patients respectively - i.e. Roque stratifies on the PCOS/ovulatory axis MORE directly than Bosdou does, not merely by proxy. The Cochrane review names both in the same breath, verbatim: 'Two recently published systematic reviews and meta-analyses, Roque 2019 and Bosdou 2019 reported a higher live birth rate after the first transfer in the freeze all strategy compared to conventional IVF/ICSI... In Roque 2019 this increased live birth rate was only found in hyper-responders and in cycles with PGT-A.' This omission is material rather than pedantic, because the claim's substantive argument is that the apparent subgroup difference is 'a difference in precision, not in effect size'. That argument is weaker once Roque is included: Roque's strata differ by 0.13 on the RR scale (1.16 versus 1.03), nearly three times Bosdou's 0.05 gap, and Roque's normo-responder interval (0.91-1.17) is tight rather than wide, so the null result there cannot be dismissed as imprecision. Everything else in the claim checks out: both relative risks and both confidence intervals are verbatim correct, the population description is correct, the timing (live birth after the FIRST frozen transfer in a freeze-only strategy) is correct, and the limitation sentence is verbatim correct - 'the analysis did not apply a standard for determining high or normal responders since the type of ovarian response followed the characterisation of populations as reported by the authors of the eligible studies'. I also independently confirm the claim's two flagged caveats: (i) WebFetch of the Bosdou full text reports that no formal test for subgroup differences, interaction test or meta-regression is present, so 'no interaction test is reported' stands; (ii) the published abstract really is internally inconsistent on stratum sizes - it states four RCTs with n=3255 in normal responders and four RCTs with n=2010 in high responders, yet the live-birth analysis reports n=3398 in high responders, which exceeds the stated high-responder total. The fix is to delete the word 'only' and add Roque 2019 as a second, concordant, earlier subgroup meta-analysis.
B_what_is_wrong: The two pooled RR estimates and confidence intervals do appear in the source, but the live-birth sample sizes printed beside them are internally impossible and assigned to the wrong populations. Table II identifies the three high-responder live-birth trials as Absalan (100), Chen (1508), and Aflatoonian (280), totaling 1888—not 3398. It identifies the three normal-responder live-birth trials as Coates (179), Shi (2157), and Vuong (782), totaling 3118—not 1608. The article separately states that all four high-responder RCTs total only 2010 participants and all four normal-responder RCTs total 3255. In addition, no cross-stratum interaction test was performed, so “a difference in precision, not in effect size” is an interpretation of similar point estimates, not a tested source result.
